nameStory: The red-berried elder gets its name from its striking bright red berries that ripen in summer, making it easy to distinguish from its black-fruited cousin. The word 'elder' comes from the Anglo-Saxon 'aeld,' meaning fire, because the hollow stems were once used to blow air into fires. These vibrant red clusters are like nature's warning lights - beautiful to look at but telling you to cook before you eat!
description: Red-berried elder is a medium-sized shrub that typically grows 6-12 feet tall with multiple stems arising from the base. It's a member of the elder family, sporting compound leaves and showy clusters of small flowers that later transform into eye-catching red berries. This hardy shrub has a somewhat wild, irregular growth habit that makes it look right at home in natural settings. The plant is largely poisonous when raw, but indigenous peoples have long known how to prepare the berries safely for food.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries arranged in pyramid-shaped clusters that ripen in mid to late summer. The berries are small drupes with a slightly wrinkled texture when ripe and have an unpleasant raw smell that warns of their toxicity.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-7 leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, each leaflet oval-shaped with serrated edges. The leaves feel somewhat rough to the touch and have a distinctive musky smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers packed densely into cone-shaped or pyramid-shaped clusters at branch tips in late spring to early summer. The flower clusters have a sweet, honey-like fragrance that attracts numerous insects.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Multi-stemmed shrub with somewhat arching branches and a tendency to form colonies through root sprouting. The bark is grayish-brown and relatively smooth on younger stems, becoming slightly furrowed with age.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are reddish-brown and distinctly scaly, arranged opposite each other along the stems. The pith inside broken twigs is notably orange to reddish-brown, which is visible even in winter identification.

habitat: Red-berried elder thrives in cool, moist areas throughout New England's mountains and northern regions. Look for it along forest edges, in clearings, near streams, and in areas that have been recently disturbed by logging or storms. It prefers acidic soils and partial shade, often growing alongside mountain ash, birches, and maples in higher elevation forests.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late April to May, unfolding their compound leaflets. The distinctive cone-shaped flower clusters appear in late May to June, filling the air with their sweet fragrance and buzzing with pollinating insects.
seasonality.summer: Flowers give way to green berries that gradually ripen to bright red by mid to late summer. The red berry clusters become the plant's most distinctive feature, glowing like natural ornaments against the green foliage.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to reddish before dropping, while some red berry clusters may persist into early fall. The multi-stemmed structure becomes more visible as leaves fall, revealing the shrub's branching pattern.
seasonality.winter: Bare stems show opposite branching with reddish-brown scaly buds. Breaking a twig reveals the diagnostic orange to reddish-brown pith inside, making winter identification possible even without leaves or fruit.

funFact: The hollow stems of red-berried elder were traditionally used by indigenous peoples to make flutes and blow-guns, earning it the nickname 'pop-gun wood' - you can actually push out the soft pith with a stick to create a natural tube!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with American black elderberry, but the red berries are a dead giveaway - black elderberry has dark purple-black berries in flat-topped clusters, while red-berried elder has bright red berries in pyramid-shaped clusters. Remember: 'Red is pyramid, black is flat.'
contextualKnowledge: While both elder species have edible berries when properly cooked, red-berried elder requires more careful preparation and is generally considered less palatable than black elderberry. The raw berries of both species can cause digestive upset, so this is definitely a 'look but don't taste' plant for casual observers.
compareHints: Red-berried elder differs from American black elderberry primarily in fruit color and cluster shape - red versus black berries, and pyramid-shaped versus flat-topped clusters. Red-berried elder also tends to prefer cooler, more mountainous habitats compared to black elderberry's preference for wetlands and lower elevations. The flower clusters also differ slightly, with red-berried elder having more cone-shaped flower heads compared to the flat-topped clusters of black elderberry.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relative red elderberry, American black elderberry grows larger, prefers wetter soils, and blooms later in the season.
